The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf r (t)$ is given by $\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] .$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] = \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $\nabla f(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-z),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-z),\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-z)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x,-2y,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x = \sin t, y=\cos t,$ and $z=t$ into the above to find $\nabla f(\mathbf r(t)){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-1⟩\cdot ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,1⟩ \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-1\cdot 1 \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1 \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)$ at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right))] & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)-1 \\  & =4\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{x}{y}\right),\frac{∂}{∂y}\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{y},-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=2t$ and $y=\sqrt{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}},-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}},-2⟩\cdot ⟨2,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}\cdot 2-2\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{t}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=9$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(9))] & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that to differentiate the $xy$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+xy & =6{y}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+xy) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6{y}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xy) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6{y}^{2}) \\ 2x+(y+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}) & =12y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\ 2x+y+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =12y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-12y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x-y \\ (x-12y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x-y \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{-2x-y}{x-12y}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(2,1)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(2,\,1)} \\  & ={\left(\frac{-2x-y}{x-12y}\right)|}_{(2,\,1)} \\  & =\frac{-2(2)-1}{2-12(1)} \\  & =\frac{(-5)}{(-10)} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}

$$

where $t \in [0,2\pi)$ and $z \in (-\infty,\infty).$

Therefore, the first component of $\mathbf{f}$ is ${\color{blue}2\cos{t}}.$

f(x,z)=⟨x,6x2,___⟩

The vector-valued function f(x,z) above parametrizes the parabolic cylinder defined in Cartesian coordinates as y=6x2. What is the third component of f?

before:
For any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,z) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨x,\,6{x}^{2},\,z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $x\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Therefore, the third component of $f$ is $z.$

source.html:
For any point (x,y,z) on our surface, we obtain the following:

f(x,z)=⟨x,y,z⟩=⟨x,6x2,z⟩

where x∈(−∞,∞) and z∈(−∞,∞).

Therefore, the third component of f is z.

The vector-valued function f(y,z) above parametrizes the parabolic cylinder defined in Cartesian coordinates as x=3y2. What is the first component of f?

before:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(y,z) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨3{y}^{2},\,y,\,z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $y\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Therefore, the first component of $f$ is $3{y}^{2}.$

The vector-valued function f(x,t) above parametrizes one sheet of the hyperbolic cylinder defined in Cartesian coordinates as y2−z2=49 for y≥7. What is the second component of f?

before:
Recall that the hyperbola ${y}^{2}-{z}^{2}=49$ for $y\ge 7$ in $yz$-plane has the parametrization

$$
⟨y,z⟩=⟨7\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,7\operatorname{tan}⁡t⟩,\,t\in (-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2})
$$

For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(1+x+y^2\right) = 1,
$$

and

$$
\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(1+x+y^2\right) = 2y.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\frac{1}{\sqrt{z-x+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂x}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{(1+x+{y}^{2})-x+{y}^{2}}}\cdot \sqrt{1+{1}^{2}+(2y)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+2{y}^{2}}}\cdot \sqrt{2+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+2{y}^{2}}}\cdot \sqrt{2(1+2{y}^{2})}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+2{y}^{2}}}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{1+2{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{1}{\cancel{\sqrt{1+2{y}^{2}}}}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \cancel{\sqrt{1+2{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot (1-0)\cdot (1-(-1)) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot 1\cdot 2 \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

n=a(t)i+b(t)j||r′(t)||. Find the function b(t).

Hint: Observe that C is traversed clockwise.

before:
For convenience, we express $r(t)$ in column vector notation:

$$
r(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}7\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 24\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}
$$

To calculate the outward normal vector of a closed, *negatively* oriented curve, we follow three steps:

**Step 1**: We compute the tangent vector ${r}^{′}(t).$

Differentiating the expression for $r(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{′}(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}7\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -24\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Since $C$ is oriented clockwise, we rotate ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ *counterclockwise* to obtain an outward normal vector.

The rotation matrix that corresponds to a ${90}^{∘}$ counterclockwise rotation is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ counterclockwise, we get

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}7\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -24\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}24\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 7\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 3**: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step $2.$

Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(t)$ (since they differ only by a rotation). Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{1}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}\begin{bmatrix}24\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 7\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}=\frac{24\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+7\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that $b(t)=7\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$

We can parameterize $C$ as follows:

$$
r(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix},\,t\in [0,2\pi )
$$

To calculate the outward-pointing normal vector of a closed, positively oriented curve, we follow three steps:

**Step 1**: We compute the tangent vector ${r}^{′}(t).$

Differentiating the expression for $r(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{′}(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Since $C$ is oriented counterclockwise, we rotate ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ *clockwise* to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

The rotation matrix that corresponds to a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise, we get

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 3**: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2.

Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(t)$ (since they differ only by a rotation).

Now, since 

$$
||{r}^{′}(t)||=\sqrt{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}}=3,
$$

and since for our curve $x(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y(t)=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ it follows that

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{1}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}.

Finally, we conclude that $b(t)=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$

We found that a parametrization of the cylinder is given by

$$
f(\theta ,z)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z⟩\,(\theta ,z)\in C.
$$

Restricting the parametrization of the cylinder to $z=2,$ we get a parametrization $r(\theta )$ for the heating element:

$$
r(\theta )=f(\theta ,2)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,2⟩
$$

For convenience, we express $r(\theta )$ in column vector column:

$$
r(\theta )=\begin{bmatrix}x(\theta ) \\ y(\theta ) \\ z(\theta )\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

 
Notice that this curve is traversed *counterclockwise* when viewed from above.

To calculate the outward-pointing unit normal vector to this curve, we follow three steps:

**Step 1:** We compute the tangent vector ${r}^{′}(\theta ).$

Differentiating the expression for $r(\theta ),$ we get

$$
{r}^{′}(\theta )=\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{′}(\theta ) \\ {y}^{′}(\theta ) \\ {z}^{′}(\theta )\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2:** Since $C$ is traversed counterclockwise, we rotate ${r}^{′}(\theta )$ by $\frac{\pi }{2}$ radians clockwise $(ϕ=-\frac{\pi }{2})$ to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

Using the hint, the rotation matrix corresponding to a $ϕ=-\frac{\pi }{2}$ counterclockwise rotation about the $z$-axis is

$$
{R}_{z}(\theta )=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(\theta )$ by $-\frac{\pi }{2}$ counterclockwise, we get

$$
\overset{~}{n}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

**Step 3:** Finally, we normalize the vector found in Step 2:

$$
\begin{aligned}||\overset{~}{n}|| & =\sqrt{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{||\overset{~}{n}||} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}x(\theta ) \\ y(\theta ) \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{x}{3}\,i+\frac{y}{3}\,j+0\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

We can parameterize $C$ as follows:

$$
r(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix},\,t\in [0,2\pi )
$$

To calculate the outward-pointing normal vector of a closed, positively oriented curve, we follow three steps:

**Step 1**: We compute the tangent vector ${r}^{′}(t).$

Differentiating the expression for $r(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{′}(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Since $C$ is oriented counterclockwise, we rotate ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ *clockwise* to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

The rotation matrix that corresponds to a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise, we get

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 3**: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2.

Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(t)$ (since they differ only by a rotation).

Now, since 

$$
||{r}^{′}(t)||=\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}}=4,
$$

and since for our curve $x(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y(t)=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ it follows that

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{1}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}\begin{bmatrix}4\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}4\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can parameterize C as follows:

r(t)=[x(t)y(t)]=[4cos⁡t4sin⁡t],t∈[0,2π)

To calculate the outward-pointing normal vector of a closed, positively oriented curve, we follow three steps:

Step 1: We compute the tangent vector r′(t).

Differentiating the expression for r(t), we get

r′(t)=[x′(t)y′(t)]=[−4sin⁡t4cos⁡t].

Step 2: Since C is oriented counterclockwise, we rotate r′(t) by 90∘ clockwise to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

The rotation matrix that corresponds to a 90∘ clockwise rotation is

[01−10].

Rotating the vector r′(t) by 90∘ clockwise, we get

[01−10][−4sin⁡t4cos⁡t]=[4cos⁡t4sin⁡t].

Step 3: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2.

Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of r′(t) (since they differ only by a rotation).

Now, since

||r′(t)||=(−4sin⁡t)2+(4cos⁡t)2=4,

and since for our curve x(t)=4cos⁡t and y(t)=4sin⁡t, it follows that

n=1||r′(t)||[4cos⁡t4sin⁡t]=14[4cos⁡t4sin⁡t]=14[xy].

$$

**Step 2**: Since $C$ is oriented counterclockwise, we rotate ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ *clockwise* to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

The rotation matrix that corresponds to a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation is

$$

Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise, we get

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \sqrt{7}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{7}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 3**: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2.

Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(t)$ (since they differ only by a rotation).

Now, since 

$$
||{r}^{′}(t)||=\sqrt{(-\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}}=\sqrt{7},
$$

and since for our curve $x(t)=\sqrt{7}\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y(t)=\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ it follows that

The area of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is the sum of the areas of the triangles $△ABD$ and $△BDC$ (see the illustration below).

![](images/cd/cd9363a3cc686ae45f49c982f4b31ad75b7c7897dcf7e8af58e530dba6946e1d.png)

First we find the area for $△ABD:$ 
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ABD} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 6\cdot 7\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{50}^{∘} \\  & =21\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{50}^{∘} \\  & ≈16.086\,9,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to four decimal places.

Now we find the area for $△BCD:$ 
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{BDC} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 7\cdot 8\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{43}^{∘} \\  & =28\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{43}^{∘} \\  & ≈19.096\,0,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to four decimal places.

Finally, we add together the areas of our two triangles to determine the area of $ABCD:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ABCD} & ={A}_{ABD}+{A}_{BDC} \\  & ≈16.086\,9+19.096\,0 \\  & ≈35.182\,9\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, to the **nearest tenth**, the area of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is $35.2.$

The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=1.$ So, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative $f_x(0,1).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $f_x(x,y)$ at $(0,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,1) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}\pi }{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(0)+\frac{\pi (1)}{4}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}\pi }{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(0,1) & ={f}_{x}(0,1)(x-0) \\ z-1 & =\frac{\pi }{4}x \\ z & =\frac{\pi }{4}x+1\end{aligned}
$$

The equation above represents a line in the $xz$-plane. The $xz$-plane through the point $P(0,1,1)$ has the equation $y=1.$

So, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(0,1,1)$ is given by the intersection of the following planes:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y &=1 \\ z &=\frac{\pi }{4}x+1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

To find a tangent vector, we can find a normal vector to each plane and compute their cross product.

- For the plane $y = 1,$ we write $0x + 1y + 0z = 1$ and find the normal vector $\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle 0,1,0 \rangle.$

- For the plane $z = \dfrac{\pi}{4} x +1,$ we write $-\dfrac{\pi}{4} x + 0y + 1z = 1$ and find the normal vector $\mathbf{n}_2 = \left\langle -\dfrac{\pi}4,0,1 \right\rangle.$

Computing the cross product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨-\frac{\pi }{4},0,1⟩ \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\pi /4 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =i+\frac{\pi }{4}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we've found a tangent vector, and this could be our final answer. However, just to make our answer a little nicer, we can multiply the vector by $4$ to yield a simpler, parallel vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot (i+\frac{\pi }{4}\,k)=4\,i+\pi \,k\end{aligned}
$$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(2,-3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(2,-3) & =6(2-1)=6\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(2,-3) & ={f}_{x}(2,-3)(x-2) \\ z-3 & =6(x-2) \\ z-3 & =6x-12 \\ z & =6x-9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,1,0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y &=-3 \\ z &=6x-9\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=-3,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=6x-9$ (or $6x-z-9=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨6,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨6,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 6 & 0 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-i-6\,k \\  & =⟨-1,0,-6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $⟨-1,0,-6⟩$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-⟨-1,0,-6⟩=⟨1,0,6⟩$ is also parallel to it.

To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

Since $\mathbf{r}(t) =t^2\, \mathbf{i} + t \,\mathbf{j} + 1 \,\mathbf{k},$ then along the curve we have $x = t^2,$ $y = t,$ and $z=1.$  

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)\,k \\  & =2t\,i+1\,j+0\,k \\  & =2t\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y,z) = \dfrac{x}{yz},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{{t}^{2}}{t\cdot 1}=t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}t\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u= 4t^2+1,$ $\textrm d u=8t\,\textrm d t$ as follows: 

$$

Here, we have $f(x,y) =  xy^3$. Along the path, we have $x=\cos t$ and $y=\sin t,$ and so we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =f(\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{3} \\  & ={sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{y}^{3}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 1\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude that

$$
\int\limits_C xy^3 \, \textrm{d}s = \int^{\pi/2}_{0} \sin^3 t \cos t \, \textrm{d}t .
$$

Computing r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖, we get the following:

r(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(4sin⁡t)i+ddt(−3sin⁡t)j=4cos⁡ti−3cos⁡tj‖r′(t)‖=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2=(4cos⁡t)2+(−3cos⁡t)2=16cos2+9cos2⁡t=25cos2⁡t=5|cos⁡t|=5cos⁡t

Notice that |cos⁡t|=cos⁡t because cos⁡t≥0 when t∈[0,π2].

Now, since f(x,y)=x2+y25, we obtain

f(r(t))=16sin2⁡t+9sin2⁡t5=25sin2⁡t5=5sin2⁡t.

Therefore, we can write the integral as

before:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $$
\displaystyle r(t)=t\,i+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\,j+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\,k,
$$ then along the curve we have $x=t,$ $y=\frac{{t}^{2}}{2},$ and $z=\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}.$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\right)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\right)\,k \\  & =i+t\,j+t\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+2{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, if $f(x,y)=\frac{y+z}{x}$, then we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}}{t}=t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{y+z}{x}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}t\sqrt{1+2{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=1+2{t}^{2}$, $\text{d}u=4t\,\text{d}t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}t\sqrt{1+2{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{3}^{5}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{3}^{5}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}\,{|}_{3}^{5} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}({5}^{3/2}-{3}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{5\sqrt{5}-3\sqrt{3}}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}+1,\,{t}^{2}-1,\,{t}^{2}⟩,$ then along the curve we have $x={t}^{2}+1,$ $y={t}^{2}-1,$ and $z={t}^{2}.$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+1)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-1)j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})k \\  & =2t\,i+2t\,j+2t\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+(2t)^{2}+(2t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+4{t}^{2}+4{t}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{12{t}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}|t| \\  & =2\sqrt{3}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|t|=t$ since $t>0$ along the path of $C.$

Now, since $f(x,y,z)=x+y-z$, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =({t}^{2}+1)+({t}^{2}-1)-{t}^{2} \\  & =2{t}^{2}-{t}^{2} \\  & ={t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{3}t\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =2\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)k \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+1} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Now, if $f(x,y,z)=z({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})$, then we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =t((\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}-(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}) \\  & =t({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as  

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}z({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

The directional derivative $g'_{\mathbf u}(a,b)$ of a function $g(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $\mathbf v$ is given by

$$
g'_{\mathbf u}(a,b) = \nabla g(a,b)\cdot\mathbf u
$$

where $\mathbf u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf v.$

First, we find the direction vector and the corresponding unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨1,4⟩-⟨0,1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,3⟩ \\ u & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{‖\overset{\to }{AB}‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}}}⟨1,3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}⟨1,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the gradient $\nabla g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $A(0,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}+4xy),\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}+4xy)⟩ \\  & =⟨6x+4y,\,4x⟩ \\ ∇g(0,1) & =⟨6\cdot 0+4\cdot 1,\,4\cdot 0⟩ \\  & =⟨4,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$

$$

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+{4}^{2}}=\sqrt{25}=5 \\ u & =\frac{1}{5}(-3\,i+4\,j)\end{aligned}
$$

In part 3, we found that the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ at the point $(1,1)$ is

$$
∇\,f(1,1)=∇(\text{div}\,V)\,{|}_{(1,\,1)}=4\,i+2\,j.
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(1,1) & =∇\,f(1,1)\cdot u \\  & =(4\,i+2\,j)\cdot (\frac{1}{5}(-3\,i+4\,j)) \\  & =\frac{4\cdot (-3)+2\cdot 4}{5} \\  & =-\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

before: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=xy$ at the point $(2,1)$ in the direction of the vector $v=\sqrt{3}\,i+j.$

source.html: Find the directional derivative of the function f(x,y)=xy at the point (2,1) in the direction of the vector v=3i+j.

before:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}}=2 \\ u & =\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{3}\,i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy)\text{ }j \\  & =y\,i+x\,j \\ ∇\,f(2,1) & =i+2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(2,1) & =∇\,f(2,1)\cdot u \\  & =(i+2\,j)\cdot \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{3}\,i+j) \\  & =\frac{1(\sqrt{3})+2(1)}{2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}+2}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

source.html:
The directional derivative fu′(a,b) of a function f(x,y) at the point (a,b) in the direction of the vector v is given by fu′(a,b)=∇f(a,b)⋅u where u is a unit vector in the direction of v.

First, we find the unit vector u in the direction of v: ‖v‖=(3)2+12=2u=12(3i+j)

Now, we compute the gradient ∇f(x,y) and evaluate it at the point (2,1):

∇f(x,y)=∂∂x(xy) i+∂∂y(xy) j=yi+xj∇f(2,1)=i+2j

Therefore, the directional derivative is fu′(2,1)=∇f(2,1)⋅u=(i+2j)⋅12(3i+j)=1(3)+2(1)2=3+22.

before:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}}=5 \\ u & =\frac{1}{5}(3\,i+4\,j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(0,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}))\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}))\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}j \\ ∇\,f(0,-1) & =\frac{2(0)}{{0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\,i+\frac{2(-1)}{{0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\,j \\  & =-2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(0,-1) & =∇\,f(0,-1)\cdot u \\  & =-2\,j\cdot \frac{1}{5}(3\,i+4\,j) \\  & =-\frac{2(4)}{5} \\  & =-\frac{8}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the unit vector u in the direction of v: ‖v‖=32+42=5u=15(3i+4j)

Now, we compute the gradient ∇f(x,y) and evaluate it at the point (0,−1): ∇f(x,y)=∂∂x(ln⁡(x2+y2)) i+∂∂y(ln⁡(x2+y2)) j=2xx2+y2i+2yx2+y2j∇f(0,−1)=2(0)02+(−1)2i+2(−1)02+(−1)2j=−2j

Therefore, the directional derivative is fu′(0,−1)=∇f(0,−1)⋅u=−2j⋅15(3i+4j)=−2(4)5=−85.

The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=\sqrt{2} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i-j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy)j \\  & =(2x-y)\,i+(2y-x)\,j \\ ∇\,f(1,1) & =(2(1)-1)\,i+(2(1)-1)\,j \\  & =i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(1,1) & =∇\,f(1,1)\cdot u \\  & =(i+j)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i-j) \\  & =\frac{1(1)+1(-1)}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int (4t+1)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =2{t}^{2}+t+C\end{aligned}

$$
0 = 2(0^2) + 0 + C
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
C = 0.

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{0} & =v(1)=2({1}^{2})+1=3\,m/s, \\ {v}_{1} & =v(2)=2({2}^{2})+2=10\,m/s.\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =Δ\,\text{KE} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot (4)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot {0}^{2} \\  & =8-0 \\  & =8\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

before:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

The particle's velocity is given by $v(t)=2t,$ where $t$ is time in seconds. So, the particle's initial velocity, at $t=1$, is

$$
{v}_{0}=v(1)=2(1)=2\,m/s,
$$

and final velocity, at $t=2$, is

$$
{v}_{1}=v(2)=2(2)=4\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =Δ\,\text{KE} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot (4)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot (2)^{2} \\  & =16-4 \\  & =12\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

The acceleration of the particle is given by $a(t)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}+1,$ where $t$ is time in seconds.
We find the velocity $v(t)$ of the particle by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{t}+t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
2=\sqrt{0}+0+C\,⟹\,C=2.
$$

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\sqrt{t}+t+2.$
In particular, the particle's initial velocity, at $t=1,$ is

$$
{v}_{0}=v(1)=\sqrt{1}+1+2=4\,m/s,
$$

and final velocity, at $t=4$, is

$$
{v}_{1}=v(4)=\sqrt{4}+4+2=8\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =Δ\,\text{KE} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 6\cdot {8}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 6\cdot {4}^{2} \\  & =192-48 \\  & =144\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

The work done by a force $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from $x={x}_{1}$ to $x={x}_{2}$ is given by

$$
W={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($J$).

Using Newton's second law of motion, the force required to accelerate a particle of mass $2.5\,kg$ at a rate of $(4-{x}^{2})\,{m/s}^{2}$ is

$$
F=ma=2.5\cdot (4-{x}^{2})=(10-2.5{x}^{2})\,N.
$$

Now, substituting the known values into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(10-2.5{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[10x-\frac{5}{6}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(10(1)-\frac{5}{6}({1}^{3}))-(10(0)-\frac{5}{6}({0}^{3})) \\  & =10-\frac{5}{6} \\  & =\frac{55}{6}\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

The closed curve $C$ is the unit circle. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \cos{t}\,\mathbf{i} + \sin{t}\,\mathbf{j},
\qquad 0 \leq t \lt 2\pi.
$$

The circulation $\Gamma$ measures the total work done by a force $\mathbf F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
\Gamma = \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm{d} \mathbf r
= \int_a^b \mathbf F(r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \; \textrm{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = \cos t, \qquad
y = \sin t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))=-y\,i+x\,j=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf r'(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=5\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i-x\,j \\  & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(-5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot 5\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-25{sin}^{2}⁡t-25{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =-25.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-25)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-25t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-25(2\pi )-0 \\  & =-50\pi \end{aligned}
$$

The circulation Γ measures the total work done by a force F in moving a particle along a closed curve C. It is given by the formula Γ=∮CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

Along the curve C, we have x=5cos⁡t,y=5sin⁡t.

So,

F(r(t))=yi−xj=5sin⁡ti−5cos⁡tj.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=ddt(5cos⁡t)i+ddt(5sin⁡t)j=−5sin⁡ti+5cos⁡tj.

Therefore,

F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(5sin⁡ti−5cos⁡tj)⋅(−5sin⁡ti+5cos⁡tj)=5sin⁡t⋅(−5sin⁡t)+(−5cos⁡t)⋅5cos⁡t=−25sin2⁡t−25cos2⁡t=−25.

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

Γ=∮CF⋅dr=∫02πF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫02π(−25)dt=−25t|02π=−25(2π)−0=−50π

If $F$ is a conservative vector field on ${R}^{2},$ then the circulation $Γ=0$ for any *closed* path $C\in {R}^{2},$ that is 

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.
$$

We notice that $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with domain $D={R}^{2}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\frac{4xy}{(1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{2}}.
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each statement in turn:

- Statement “$F$ is conservative” is true. The vector field $F$ is conservative since the partial derivatives are equal and continuous everywhere on ${R}^{2}.$

- Statement “$$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0
$$ for any piecewise smooth path $C\in {R}^{2}$” is false, while statement “$$
\displaystyle {∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0
$$ for any closed path $C\in {R}^{2}$” is true. The result $Γ=0$ applies to closed curves only.

Therefore, the correct answer is “$F$ is conservative”; “$$
\displaystyle {∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0
$$ for any closed path $C\in {R}^{2}$” only.

before:
First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is the ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $1$ and $5,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=5\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\frac{5}{y}\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i+\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i+\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot 5\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-1+5 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4\,\text{d}t \\  & =4t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =4(2\pi )-0 \\  & =8\pi \end{aligned}
$$

source.html:
The circulation Γ measures the total work done by a force F in moving a particle along a closed curve C. It is given by the formula Γ=∮CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

We now recall the following:

  • If the force works with the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ∮CF⋅dr>0.

  • If the force works against the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ∮CF⋅dr<0.

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

  • Statement I is false, while statement II is true. Since the force F acts perpendicular to the motion of the particle as it moves around C, it neither helps nor hinders its motion.
    So, ∮CF⋅dr=0.
  • Statement III is false. If we reverse the orientation of C, then the situation with regards to the work done by F remains unchanged.
    So, ∮−CF⋅dr=0.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =-y\,i+x\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =2{sin}^{2}⁡t+2{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }2\,\text{d}t \\  & =2t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =2(2\pi )-0 \\  & =4\pi \end{aligned}
$$

before:
First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is the ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $3$ and $1,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =2x\,i+2y\,j \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

before:
If $F$ is a conservative vector field on ${R}^{2},$ then the circulation $Γ=0$ for any *closed* path $C\in {R}^{2},$ that is 

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.
$$

We notice that $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with domain $D={R}^{2}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={e}^{x+y}.
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each statement in turn:

- Statement “$F$ is **not** conservative” is false. The vector field $F$ is conservative since the partial derivatives are equal and continuous everywhere on ${R}^{2}.$

- Statement “$$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0
$$ for any piecewise smooth path $C\in {R}^{2}$” is false. The result $Γ=0$ applies to closed curves only.

- Statement “$$
\displaystyle {∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r\ne 0
$$ for some closed paths $C\in {R}^{2}$” is false. The circulation $Γ=0$ for any closed path $C\in {R}^{2}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true."

L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6}\sqrt{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6}\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6}1\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\theta {|}_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6} \\  & =2(\frac{5\pi }{6}-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\theta ).
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /12}\sqrt{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ))^{2}+(-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /12}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡(6\theta )+36{sin}^{2}⁡(6\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{5+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4+8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{8+8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{8}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall the identity for $\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{x}{2}\right):$

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)=\sqrt{\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}}
$$

Therefore, using $x=\theta $ in the previous identity, the integral can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2{cos}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\theta }{2}\right)}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\theta }{2}\right)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={4\cdot 2(\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\theta }{2}\right))|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =8(\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{(5-5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{25-50\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +25{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +25{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{25-50\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +25}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{50-50\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{50}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}

Now, we recall the identity for $\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{x}{2}\right):$

The gradient of the function $f(x,y)$ is defined as

$$
\nabla f(x,y) = \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}}\,\textbf{i} + \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}}\,\textbf{j}.
$$

Since $\nabla f(x,y) = \mathbf F(x,y),$ the function $f(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}} = 2xy, \qquad \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} = x^2-3.
$$

First, we integrate $\dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int 2xy\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}y+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} = x^2 + g'(y).
$$

Taking $\dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} = x^2 -3$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{g}^{′}(y) & ={x}^{2}-3 \\ {g}^{′}(y) & =-3 \\ g(y) & =-3y+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)=-3y +C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y) = x^2y -3y + C.
$$

The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
\nabla f(x,y,z) = \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}} \, \mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} \, \mathbf{j} + \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{z}} \, \mathbf{k}.
$$

Since $\nabla f(x,y,z)  = \mathbf{F}(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}} = yz, \qquad \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} = xz + 4z^2, \qquad \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{z}} = xy+8yz.
$$

First, we integrate $\dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int yz\,\text{d}x \\  & =xyz+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} = xz + \dfrac{\partial{g}}{\partial{y}}.
$$

Taking $\dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} = xz + 4z^2$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}xz+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =xz+4{z}^{2} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =4{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\dfrac{\partial{g}}{\partial{y}}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int 4{z}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =4y{z}^{2}+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z) = 4yz^2 + h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x, y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z) = xyz + 4yz^2 + h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{z}} = xy + 8yz + h'(z).
$$

Taking $\dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{z}} = xy+8yz$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}xy+8yz & =xy+8yz+{h}^{′}(z) \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ h(z) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z) = xyz + 4yz^2 + C.
$$

before: Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ where $F(x,y,z)=(2xz+\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,i+x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,j+{x}^{2}\,k.$

source.html: Find f(x,y,z) such that ∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z), where F(x,y,z)=(2xz+sin⁡y)i+xcos⁡yj+x2k.

before:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,k.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2xz+\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}={x}^{2}
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (2xz+\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}z+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int 0\,\text{d}y \\  & =h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}z+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}={x}^{2}+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}={x}^{2}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+{h}^{′}(z) \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ h(z) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}z+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+C.
$$

before:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{i}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,\text{j}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,\text{k}.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}={y}^{2}{z}^{3}-{e}^{z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2xy{z}^{3},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z}
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int ({y}^{2}{z}^{3}-{e}^{z})\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}-x{e}^{z}+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2xy{z}^{3}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2xy{z}^{3}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2xy{z}^{3}+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =2xy{z}^{3} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int 0\,\text{d}y \\  & =h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}-x{e}^{z}+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}=3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z}+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z}+{h}^{′}(z) & =3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z} \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ h(z) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

\begin{aligned}xy{e}^{xz}+x+{h}^{′}(z) & =zy{e}^{xz}+x \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ h(z) & =C,\end{aligned}

Consequently,

$$

$$

source.html:
The gradient of the function f(x,y,z) is defined as ∇f(x,y,z)=∂f∂xi+∂f∂yj+∂f∂zk.

Since ∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z), the function f(x,y,z) must satisfy the following system: ∂f∂x=yzexz+z,∂f∂y=exz+1,∂f∂z=xyexz+x

First, we integrate ∂f∂x with respect to x. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of y and z: f(x,y,z)=∫∂f∂xdx=∫(yzexz+z)dx=yexz+xz+g(y,z)

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to y, we obtain ∂f∂y=exz+∂g∂y

Taking ∂f∂y=exz+1 into account, we obtain exz+∂g∂y=exz+1∂g∂y=1

Now we integrate ∂g∂y with respect to y. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of z: g(y,z)=∫∂g∂ydy=∫1dy=y+h(z)

Substituting g(y,z)=y+h(z) in the expression for f(x,y,z), we get f(x,y,z)=yexz+xz+y+h(z).

To determine the function h(z), we differentiate f(x,y,z) with respect to z. This gives ∂f∂z=xyexz+x+h′(z).

Taking ∂f∂z=xyexz+x into account, we obtain xyexz+x+h′(z)=zyexz+xh′(z)=0h(z)=C, where C is a constant.

Consequently, f(x,y,z)=yexz+xz+y+C.

Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y 
= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\textrm d A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/a7/a78a98750e3203760d27daaebd42852198538935e2c3777a0b8a8c85d1bb0901.png)

We have that $P(x,y)= \cos{y}$ and $Q(x,y)= x\sin{y}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,dx+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x,y) = 2\sin{y}.$

$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

$$

$$

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{3}+2{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=4y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$

$$

Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

 

![](images/e4/e48034aed1f41cf1f9b30c057186879233fe05cd2ba720dcee436398a732b6ce.png)

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,dx+(x-{e}^{-{y}^{2}})\,dy
$$

We have that $P(x,y)=y\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and $Q(x,y)=x-{e}^{-{y}^{2}}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,dx+(x-{e}^{-{y}^{2}})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/c2/c2e08c233cb31124234ab6e5179998a3bdc148024632c7770bdea46cd37dff83.png)

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,dx+(xy-2y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,dy
$$

We have that $P(x,y)={y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $Q(x,y)=xy-2y\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=y+2y\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le 1,\,x-1\le y\le -2x+2\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,dx+(xy-2y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(y+2y\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2y\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{x-1}^{-2x+2}y\text{ }dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$
